Port Electrification Is Becoming an Operating-System Problem

Port electrification is usually presented through the machines: battery-electric yard tractors, top handlers, forklifts, cranes, drayage trucks, and rows of charging dispensers. Those assets provide the photographs, grant totals, and equipment counts.

By Bottleneck Briefs · Published 2026-07-24 · 17 min read

In brief

  • 53 active Clean Ports grants have moved electrification into repeatable procurement.
  • Los Angeles plans 213 MVA of new capacity by 2030.
  • Terminal dispatch, utility schedules, and charger uptime now determine usable fleet capacity.
  • Managed charging could reduce construction while increasing software and workflow control.
  • The thesis fails if fleets scale with only ordinary terminal infrastructure.

The visible machines are only the first procurement

Program map or award graphic

Active Clean Ports grants connect vehicle procurement with charging, shore power, storage, and supporting infrastructure.

Open source visual from U.S. EPA

Reuse: U.S. federal government page; embedded-asset rights not separately stated · Attribution: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency

The more consequential industrial change sits behind them. Large electric fleets require ports to synchronize utility service, medium-voltage distribution, civil construction, charger commissioning, energy controls, maintenance, and terminal dispatch. An awarded vehicle becomes productive cargo capacity only when that entire chain works during the terminal’s operating window.

That makes this an ecosystem-expansion story at the repeatable-procurement stage. Ports are no longer buying isolated demonstrations. They are issuing utility-related civil packages, terminal-electrification engineering contracts, charging infrastructure solicitations, program-management assignments, and proposed long-duration service agreements.

The narrower thesis matters. Electric fleets do not mechanically require proportional grid expansion at every site. Some terminals may have spare capacity, flexible dwell periods, storage, or enough scheduling freedom to avoid major feeder work. The common requirement is coordination: ports must deliver enough power, through an operable charging system, at the times cargo equipment needs it.

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s active Clean Ports portfolio provides a useful test bed. As of June 2026, it contained 53 grants totaling approximately $2.94 billion, including 25 zero-emission technology projects worth about $2.8 billion. The portfolio covers more than 1,500 pieces of cargo-handling equipment and more than 1,000 drayage trucks, with most projects expected to implement over three or four years. (EPA Clean Ports awards)

That timetable compresses vehicle procurement, utility planning, permitting, construction, commissioning, and early operating evidence into the same period. The result will show whether port electrification creates a durable operating layer or remains a collection of grant-funded equipment purchases.

Five ports reveal five versions of the same transition

The projects differ in utility structure, terminal ownership, equipment mix, and disclosure quality. That variation is useful because it separates the general mechanism from any single engineering solution.

PortCurrent funded or proposed scopePower and infrastructure signalCurrent state

Oakland663 vehicles and equipment units, 213 charging stations, six battery systemsPort-owned public utility; seven charging sites; active terminal solicitationsRepeatable procurement under way
Baltimore213 vehicles and equipment units, 149 EVSE, 17.076 MW chargingBGE feeders, duct banks, transformers, switches, and a planned 5 MW rerouteDetailed application scope; execution evidence pending
San Diego77 grant-funded assets; proposed 70-port truck hubLegacy 12 kV loop, 1.75 MW solar, proposed 2.5 MW/5 MWh batteryPublic project plus proposed private service model

Figures come from current EPA, port, utility, and grant-application records. Project quantities are planned or awarded unless described as operating.

Los Angeles shows the physical scale most clearly. Its current terminal page lists 383 zero-emission cargo-handling units, more than 300 chargers, and 250 drayage trucks across APM Terminals, Everport, Fenix Marine Services, TraPac, Yusen Terminals, and Wallenius Wilhelmsen.

The city’s Zero-Emission Port Electrification and Operations program connects that fleet plan to the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power. A May 2026 Harbor Department action described 213 MVA of additional 34.5 kV capacity by 2030 and another 306 MVA by 2035. The department also approved a $10 million change order to install utility conduits and vaults while another port construction project was already under way. (Los Angeles ZEPEO record)

Those figures describe planned capacity, not delivered power. The distinction is important. Los Angeles had also cited 424 cargo-handling units in a January 2025 board record, while its current terminal allocations total 383. The present figure should govern; the earlier estimate shows how project scope can change before commissioning.

Oakland represents a different institutional model. The port operates its own public electric utility for maritime, aviation, and commercial customers. That structure can shorten organizational handoffs, but it does not eliminate engineering, construction, charger integration, testing, or operating coordination.

Oakland’s project combines 475 drayage trucks, 118 yard tractors, 57 forklifts, eight top picks, four reach stackers, and one railcar mover. Its application also lists 213 charging stations, six battery systems, one solar installation, and seven charging-infrastructure sites. Current terminal solicitations include electrification engineering and construction-management work at TraPac and charger, conduit, vault, switchgear, and transformer scope at SSA’s Berth 63. (Oakland procurements)

Baltimore provides the clearest application-stage link between fleet deployment and named utility work. The Maryland Port Administration describes 149 EVSE units and 17.076 MW of charging capacity, supported by feeders and duct banks from Baltimore Gas and Electric facilities to Dundalk and Seagirt.

At Seagirt, the plan pairs 90 terminal tractors with 45 chargers and 90 dispensers. The application reported approximately 10 MW available, about 5.7 MW already in use, and a BGE commitment to reroute another 5 MW. That final figure remains an applicant-reported commitment rather than delivered capacity. (Baltimore project narrative)

San Diego combines public infrastructure with an attempted service model. Its approximately $58.6 million award, plus about $28 million in matching resources, covers 77 vehicles and equipment units, shore power, and completion of a legacy 12 kV loop.

Separately, the proposed Tidelands Avenue truck hub would place 70 charging ports on 4.8 acres, supported by 1.75 MW of solar and a 2.5 MW/5 MWh battery. The project team has described private financing, engineering, installation, operation, maintenance, trial vehicles, and a five-year vehicle-ownership path. The project still requires environmental, lease, permit, financing, and customer decisions. The Tidelands hub is a proposed commercial structure, not an operating site. (San Diego Tidelands hub)

Virginia supplies a smaller operating counterexample. The port placed four electric MAFI yard tractors into service at Norfolk International Terminals in January 2023 and has since reported additional electric equipment. That proves some electric cargo machinery can operate without a publicly disclosed utility-scale expansion tied to the deployment.

Virginia’s current Clean Ports award is approximately $313.4 million. Earlier federal and port materials used roughly $380 million, and the port’s dashboard continued to carry that legacy value alongside a claim of more than 400 electric assets. The current federal award should be used for the program total; the broader asset claim remains unreconciled.

The operating gate appears after equipment adoption

The sequence is what makes this transition industrially significant.

A terminal first translates equipment counts, shifts, dwell periods, and task energy into a site-load forecast. The utility or port power department then determines available capacity, voltage, protection requirements, meter configuration, feeder work, and construction responsibilities.

Engineers convert those decisions into duct banks, vaults, switchgear, transformers, chargers, communications, and civil packages. Commissioning teams must then prove that the electrical system, chargers, software, and equipment operate together.

Only after those steps does terminal dispatch face the practical question: which machine charges, where, for how long, and without disrupting a vessel, rail transfer, gate operation, or labor schedule?

This is a sequential gate. Large grants can overcome the first adoption barrier by funding equipment. That success exposes the harder coordination problem behind the vehicles. Ports encounter the operating layer precisely because they have moved beyond a small demonstration.

The weakest link is not always utility capacity. A terminal may avoid a feeder upgrade through managed charging, storage, lower simultaneous demand, staged fleet delivery, or longer dwell windows. In that case, control shifts toward telemetry, state-of-charge forecasting, dispatch integration, and energy-management software.

NREL’s heavy-duty depot research illustrates the relief mechanism. Under its modeled assumptions, 78% to 86% of 36 substations could serve 100 trucks charging at 100 kW without an upgrade. Managed charging increased the result to about 90%. Port equipment has different duty cycles and site constraints, so the result cannot be transferred directly. It still invalidates any rule that fleet size automatically determines grid-construction spending. (NREL managed charging)

The ecosystem can therefore expand through different combinations. One terminal may build feeders and substations. Another may purchase storage and orchestration software. A third may stage vehicles or rely on a shared charging hub. The commercial constant is the need to convert electricity into completed cargo tasks on schedule.

Spend is broadening, but durable margins remain unproven

The current projects already show budget expansion beyond vehicles. Los Angeles has utility-related civil construction and grant-administration spending. Oakland is procuring engineering and infrastructure while incorporating batteries, solar, leasing, truck-as-a-service, and loaner programs. Baltimore separates electrical construction, utility work, chargers, monitoring, and equipment-support packages. San Diego is attempting to bundle land, power, vehicles, financing, and maintenance.

That does not establish where attractive economics will settle.

Civil and electrical contractors can receive large contracts without gaining durable customer control. Charger suppliers can book hardware revenue while facing competitive pricing, warranty costs, and replacement risk. Utilities may recover distribution spending while retaining monopoly control over service dates and tariffs. Software providers may gain recurring revenue only if terminals buy independent platforms rather than use charger-native tools or internal systems.

The strongest potential control points are schedule authority, land, data, workflow integration, and the customer relationship.

Utilities and port power departments control service studies, energization, tariffs, and operating limits. Port authorities control common corridors, land, permits, and tenant requirements. Terminal operators retain dispatch, labor, cargo sequencing, and final responsibility for productive shifts.

A charging or fleet-service platform could acquire a larger role by bundling capital, vehicles, charging, maintenance, and billing. Yet that model must still prove utilization, customer retention, financing terms, and renewal. An announced hub or lease structure is evidence of commercial experimentation, not durable value capture.

Existing incumbents have strong defenses. Equipment manufacturers and dealer networks can add electric models, warranties, parts, financing, and service. Utilities can move upstream into fleet planning and managed charging. Terminal maintenance departments can internalize electrical and charger work. Established engineering firms can use active-terminal experience to retain integration contracts.

Public-company exposure therefore sits across existing institutions rather than a clean group of new specialists. Konecranes supplies operating electric mobile harbor cranes in San Diego. Exelon’s Baltimore Gas and Electric is the named utility counterpart in Maryland. Dominion Energy has the existing utility relationship in Virginia. ICF received a Los Angeles grant-administration authorization. UL Solutions provides relevant charging-safety and certification capabilities. These are exposures to specific functions, not evidence that port electrification is financially material to any company.

Standards can open the stack—or formalize lock-in

Charging interoperability will influence who controls the operating layer.

The Open Charge Alliance reports that OCPP 2.0.1 became IEC 63584 in 2024 and that OCPP 2.1 was released in 2025. OCPP 1.6 and 2.0.1 are not natively compatible, while smart-charging, security, and ISO 15118 functions depend on selected profiles and implementation.

A port using several charger vendors across multiple terminals must decide which devices a central platform can monitor and dispatch, who owns the credentials, which party can update firmware, and whether data can move when a vendor is replaced.

Open standards can reduce switching costs and support independent integration, testing, and cybersecurity services. They do not guarantee openness. A port may still select one vendor, accept proprietary extensions, leave data inside a closed platform, or require expensive integration to change systems.

The five projects reviewed do not disclose a common OCPP version, certification profile, central data architecture, or switching-right provision. The standards layer is therefore commercially available but not yet visibly embedded in port procurement.

The first material charger solicitation that names an OCPP version, certification profile, data-portability requirement, or equivalent open interface will be an important signal. It would show that ports have begun to procure architecture and control rights, rather than hardware alone.

Shore power is the closest operating precedent

California’s at-berth regulation provides the clearest historical base rate.

The state approved its original shore-power regulation in 2007 and expanded the system in 2020. Additional vessel categories entered compliance requirements in 2023 and 2025, with another milestone scheduled for 2027. California reported compliance above 95% for 2024.

The program did not end when ports installed plugs. It required vessel capability, electrical systems, connection procedures, trained personnel, reporting, exceptions, maintenance, and enforcement. Storm damage at the Port of Hueneme impaired shore-power capability. California also reached a roughly $2.2 million settlement with Matson over 2,910 alleged violations during 2020–2022. (CARB at-berth program)

The similarity is the durable operating apparatus around maritime electricity. The difference is mobility. A vessel typically connects during a defined berth call. Yard tractors, forklifts, top handlers, and drayage trucks move through overlapping shifts and variable cargo cycles. Their charging system must coordinate many mobile loads rather than one connection event.

Airport ground-equipment electrification offers another comparison. The FAA’s Voluntary Airport Low Emissions program has supported repeated charging and ground-equipment projects since 2004, including projects that were later modified or cancelled. Public funding can create a long procurement cycle, but it does not eliminate project attrition or guarantee high utilization.

These precedents support the operating-layer thesis while narrowing it. Infrastructure, procedures, maintenance, and reporting tend to persist after installation. Their existence does not prove that independent suppliers capture high margins or that every planned asset becomes productive.

The strongest counterargument is that infrastructure may outrun demand

The central thesis fails if the real pacing problem sits upstream.

Ports can construct charging sites while carriers delay vehicle adoption. Service providers can finance hubs that fail to secure sufficient throughput. Equipment can arrive but perform fewer hours than assumed. Grants can cover initial capital while leaving unfavorable electricity costs, residual values, maintenance burdens, or labor constraints unresolved.

The current evidence is much stronger on awards and planned systems than on use. Comparable public data on charger availability, charging energy, maximum coincident demand, equipment hours, cargo tasks, spare ratios, downtime, and cost per operating hour remain absent across the five projects.

Scope revisions already show that announcements are not final operating facts. Los Angeles’s current cargo-handling count is lower than its earlier board estimate. Virginia’s active award is materially below its legacy public figure. San Diego’s hub remains proposed. Baltimore’s utility work remains application-stage. Oakland’s commercial structures do not disclose pricing or renewals.

A second counterargument is that the transition may succeed without creating a large independent service market. Ports, terminal operators, utilities, OEMs, and incumbent contractors can internalize most functions. Closed charger systems can operate. Existing maintenance organizations can absorb the installed base. Utilities can manage power without ceding customer control to a software platform.

This would not stop electrification. It would change where value and authority reside.

The thesis should therefore be stated narrowly: large electric-port deployments are generating repeatable procurement for an operating layer, but neither major utility expansion nor external high-margin value capture is universal.

The next transition is from procurement to operating evidence

The current state is repeatable procurement. Moving to early scaled operation requires a different class of proof.

By 2027, the clearest sign of progress will be project-specific engineering, utility, charger, and construction awards across several ports. By 2028, at least one project should be able to pair actual energized capacity with a charger commissioning date in the same official record.

Between 2027 and 2030, managed charging or storage should begin to produce quantified effects on peak demand, utility scope, or fleet commissioning. By 2029, recurring maintenance or energy-management arrangements should extend beyond construction acceptance if a durable service layer is forming.

The stronger commercialization test arrives later. Oakland or San Diego must show a contract renewal, repeat site, or fleet expansion under a service model. At least one port should eventually authorize follow-on procurement using measured utilization, cost, availability, or cargo-performance evidence from the current program.

Those outcomes would show that ports are learning from operation and buying again. Without them, the current cycle may remain a large but temporary wave of subsidy-supported implementation.

What to watch

  • By December 2027, count ports awarding project-specific electrical, utility, charger, or construction packages.
  • By December 2028, find one official record pairing energized capacity with charger commissioning.
  • By December 2028, determine the final disposition of Baltimore’s planned 5 MW BGE reroute.
  • By December 2029, identify two recurring O&M agreements extending beyond construction acceptance.
  • By December 2030, test whether Los Angeles records a material milestone for its first 213 MVA phase.
  • By December 2031, find a follow-on procurement explicitly citing measured operating performance.

Port electrification will continue to be photographed as a vehicle transition. Its industrial outcome will be decided elsewhere: in utility agreements, construction schedules, charger uptime, terminal dispatch, service contracts, and the first credible operating datasets.

The thesis remains worth tracking because procurement has already broadened beyond machines. It remains narrow because the market has not yet shown who captures durable economics—or whether many terminals can solve the problem using existing capacity and incumbent organizations.
